title: Ang 578–584: the Alahnian
tomorrow: what happened when the herons tried to swim like the swans?

cards: The sympathy-card aisle runs on a short list of soft words: sorry, loss, thinking of you. Guru Nanak's songs for the dead, the Alahnian, open on ang 578 with a word you won't find on any of those cards. Blessed.
Blessed is the Creator, the true King, who set the whole world to its work. That's today's puzzle. Why would a dirge begin with praise?

teach.b: Start with the form. Alahnian were laments, the mourning songs of Punjab, and Guru Nanak sets his in Vadhans, a few pages after the wedding-horse songs. Same raga, the horse and the grave.
Whoever has come must rise and go; this world is a passing show.

teach.h: DON'T CALL DEATH BAD, IF YOU KNOW HOW.
teach.b: Then, on ang 579, the line people quote: don't call death bad, people, if you know how to truly die. Dying well, in these songs, means having lived toward the True One, serving and remembering, so the road ahead is open.
And there's the answer to the puzzle. The praise comes first because it sets the death inside something bigger: the same Creator who started the world and its work is the one the soul returns to.
The opening word doesn't cancel the grief. These are still songs for the dead, sung where people mourn.
What it does is give the grief a floor to stand on.

A gentle note for parents: today's lesson is about death, so a younger listener might want you nearby. Worth knowing: in the Granth, the raga that holds the wedding songs holds the funeral songs too, a few pages apart.

how: At Sikh funerals and in the days after, families gather for kirtan and a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; Guru Nanak's Alahnian in Vadhans are among the hymns that speak to death.

s: 'don't call death bad' means don't be sad at a funeral
the line is about knowing how to die, having lived toward the True One. it sits inside songs of mourning.
Guru Nanak's dirges are set in the same raga as the wedding-horse songs
both are in Vadhans, a few pages apart.
the dirges open by naming the death and the loss
they open with praise: blessed is the Creator, the true King, who set the world to its work.

games.q: a coworker's father has died. she asks why her Sikh friend's family sang hymns of praise at the service. what fits the Alahnian?
o: the praise sets the loss inside the Creator's world; it doesn't cancel the grief.
praise means the family isn't allowed to feel sad about it.
the hymns are only for weddings; the family must have mixed them up.
games.why: Guru Nanak's dirges begin with blessed is the Creator, then sing that all who come must go. they're still songs of mourning.

practice: Take a pen and paper and write the name of someone you miss, or someone grieving right now. Under it, write one true thing about how that person lived or loves.
Rest your hand on the page for the rest of the sit and let the name be there with you.
